One-sentence judgment: audio and video technicians do not "carry equipment"; they set up, test, operate, and strike audio and video equipment according to program or event requirements, verify the signal chain stage by stage, stand watch at the mixing console and switcher during performances and recordings, troubleshoot faults, and record changes. On the U.S. side this corresponds to O*NET-SOC 27-4011.00, listed as Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to below 7.0). The core boundary is this: you may operate and service equipment and follow the technical process according to the plan, but you cannot replace the director's or organizer's artistic or content decisions, and you must not record, copy, or distribute other people's performances or works without authorization.

Signals to keep exploring: you are willing to look at the signal flow and interfaces before touching anything, can stand for long periods and carry equipment and accept night work and on-site environments; when you encounter an abnormality in power, rigging, grounding, or connections, you are willing to stop and report first rather than connecting the equipment; and your interest in "is this audio clean, is this signal chain reproducible, and is the material authorization clear" is greater than in "how many videos I delivered today".

Conditions for pausing high investment: you have not yet completed one full cycle under mentoring from requirement confirmation, setup and stage-by-stage testing, on-site watch duty, and fault handling through to strike and records, or you only want to press buttons and are unwilling to learn the signal chain and safety procedures; also do not treat "knowing how to use editing software" or "having shot videos for friends" as proof that you can independently take charge of a live audio and video system.

Education, qualifications, and position authorization must be checked separately: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Three, and among respondents 43% think a bachelor's degree is required, 25% think a high school diploma or equivalent is required, and 20% think a postsecondary certificate is required; different employers vary widely in their experience and portfolio requirements. In mainland China, performing others' works, recording performances, and producing audio and video recordings involve the licensing and remuneration rules of the Copyright Law of the People's Republic of China, and the authorization for electricity use, rigging, and on-site work in a specific position is determined by the employing unit and the competent department's rules.

This page covers audio and video technicians (27-4011): equipment setup, operation, and troubleshooting, with usable signals and test and change records as outputs. They are counted separately from broadcast, sound engineering, and lighting technicians; the average wage for the related Chinese industry serves only to check the employer's background and does not stand in for this occupation's wage.

The work of this occupation can be divided into three categories: first, preparation and setup (checking the equipment list, power supply and signal interfaces, cabling, and rigging conditions against the requirements and the site plan, and completing setup with stage-by-stage testing); second, operation and troubleshooting (standing watch at the mixing console and switcher, controlling on-site lighting and sound, switching video sources, diagnosing and handling media system faults, and maintaining monitoring during a performance or meeting); third, strike and recording (striking and counting equipment, completing routine cleaning and maintenance, reporting equipment that needs major repair, and organizing materials and equipment change records and handing them over). All three share the same reproducible chain of technical records.
Preparation and setup

Check the requirements and the site plan → count the equipment and cables and inspect their appearance → confirm the power capacity, grounding, and cable routing → set up according to the signal flow and test stage by stage → confirm the rigging and elevated placement conditions → confirm the process and timing with the organizer or director.
Operation and troubleshooting

Stand watch at the mixing console and switcher according to the process → control on-site lighting and sound → switch video sources and recording status → monitor and judge abnormalities → locate and eliminate the fault or switch to a backup channel → record the change and notify the relevant positions.

Strike and count equipment and cables from the checklist, complete routine cleaning and maintenance, report equipment that needs major repair, organize recorded materials and equipment change records, and hand over to the next shift or the warehouse with an explanation of outstanding problems.

Audio and video technicians face event and recording systems; broadcast technicians face broadcasting and transmission; sound engineering technicians record, synchronize, mix, or reproduce sound for performances, film, television, and similar work, and their work is not limited to the studio; electrical and electronic engineering technicians usually handle circuits and devices under the direction of engineers; computer support and editing directions focus on information systems and finished films respectively. The actual division of labor follows the job description.
Core purpose

Under conditions that meet the electricity, rigging, and site safety requirements, make sound and picture audible, visible, switchable, and reproducible during an event or recording, and keep technical changes and fault handling as traceable records.
Main objects and basis

The objects are equipment such as microphones, mixing consoles, speakers, cables and interfaces, switchers, cameras, monitors, and servers, as well as the on-site signal chain, power and rigging conditions, recorded materials, and the equipment ledger; the basis is the event or program requirements, the equipment technical manuals and signal flow, the site's electricity and rigging rules, and the on-site safety and material authorization requirements.
Core process

Requirement and site checking, equipment counting and inspection, setup and stage-by-stage testing, on-site watch duty and monitoring, fault location and handling, strike and counting, and maintenance reporting and record handover.
Main outputs

A reproducible audio and video signal and channel list, equipment and signal test records, fault and change handling records, a description of the recorded materials and storage locations, and the counted equipment ledger.
Responsible party

Technicians take on setup, operation, and recording according to the position division of labor; the scope of content and artistic involvement is checked against the actual tasks and the organizer's or director's division of labor. The site, the unit, and the corresponding workers each perform their own responsibilities, and a permit from the organizer alone does not replace all statutory requirements. Special operations within the Chinese catalog are governed by Ministry of Emergency Management Order No. 19, effective 2026-06-01: Articles 3 and 4 require identification according to the catalog and training, assessment, and certification, and Article 36 requires the unit to verify that certificates are genuine and valid and to keep files. Whether a task falls under the catalog's electrician or work-at-height operations must be checked against the specific task; site approval and AV proficiency cannot replace statutory certificates, nor are ordinary signal cable connections all called special operations.
Authority and approval

Whether you can change the signal flow, whether you can use a backup channel, and whether you can record and store materials are determined by the event plan, the site conditions, and the material authorization agreement; operating authority comes from position authorization and training records and does not arise by itself from proficiency or seniority. Whether a task falls under the catalog's electrician or work-at-height operations must be checked against the specific task; site approval and AV proficiency cannot replace statutory certificates, nor are ordinary signal cable connections all called special operations.
Boundary of conclusions

A test record states that "this setup was completed according to the plan and verified stage by stage"; it does not equal the overall success of the event, nor does it replace a professional inspection conclusion on electricity and rigging, and it is affected by site conditions, equipment status, and changes in the on-site flow.

Before starting the job, check at least six items: the position basis and form of employment (full-time, project-based, or outsourced), the actual working hours (frequency of night and weekend work), the equipment and safety training arrangements, the scope of authorization for electricity and rigging work, the material and likeness authorization agreement, and the real method of pay (hourly, daily, or project settlement) and the overtime settlement rules.
Occupational basis

Insufficient evidence: a one-to-one mapping of the Chinese occupational classification has still not been verified; the frozen identity for this page is 27-4011.00 Audio and Video Technicians. The current O*NET 2025 industry structure: arts, entertainment, and recreation 14%, information 14%, real estate and rental and leasing 14%, other services 12%, educational services 11%, other 35%. This describes the industries in which U.S. 27-4011 employment falls, not Chinese employment, within-industry occupational wages, or equipment adoption rates. BLS27-4010 also includes broadcast 27-4012, sound 27-4014, and lighting 27-4015, and the values are not interchangeable.
Education and training path

O*NET Job Zone Three/SVP6.0 to below 7.0; the education question asks about the education new hires need, and 43% answered a bachelor's degree, 25% a high school equivalent, and 20% a postsecondary certificate, which is not the educational composition of workers. The Job Zone one to two years of training is a cross-occupation zone description, not a fixed period for this occupation. The typical entry for BLS27-4011 is a postsecondary non-degree award, no related work experience, and short-term on-the-job training; the specific position still requires checking the posting and the equipment training.
Methods and tools

The O*NET Hot Technologies single page lists 15 specific software skills: Zoom 9%, Teams 8%, Office 7%, Excel and Webex 4% each, PowerPoint and Outlook 3% each, Word 2%, and the rest below 1% or with no ratio provided. The ratios come from unique U.S. job postings associated with this occupation throughout 2025; the details profile lists a separate 15 software categories with several examples, the two are not the same count, and neither indicates an adoption rate or AI substitution.
Safety and work permits

The work involves temporary power and cable routing, equipment rigging and elevated placement, noise exposure, and night work; check the temporary power capacity and grounding, cable pathway protection, rigging point load capacity and fall protection measures, and the necessary hearing protection and lighting arrangements, and confirm which tasks must be carried out by qualified personnel.
Training and regulatory requirements

In mainland China, Articles 38, 39, 42, and 43 of the Copyright Law (2020 amendment) respectively concern the performance of works, the licensing of recording and disseminating performances, the making of audio and video recordings of works, and contractual remuneration with performers. The rights in the work and the rights of the performer are checked separately, and exceptions provided elsewhere in the law must also be verified; position competence does not automatically bring the right to use materials. Portraits and minors are checked separately according to the specific situation.
Pay and work hours

The BLS combined group is usually full-time and describes overtime and night, weekend, and holiday arrangements; this is not used to assert that the precise audio and video occupation is generally paid per project. Editorial comparison suggestion: check employment versus project settlement, standby and overtime, travel and accommodation, equipment costs, and credit and use of materials separately, and finally judge by the real contract and jurisdiction.

Audio and Video Technicians (U.S. side O*NET-SOC 27-4011.00) set up, maintain, and strike audio and video equipment for live or recorded events, including microphones, speakers, connecting cables, mixing and switching equipment, cameras, monitors, and servers and related electronic equipment, serving concerts, conferences, exhibitions, presentations, podcasts, press conferences, and sporting events. Daily work includes checking equipment and interfaces against requirements, setting up and testing the signal chain stage by stage, standing watch at the mixing console and video switcher, diagnosing and handling media system faults, controlling on-site lighting and sound, recording and editing audio materials, compressing and storing audio and video data, and completing routine cleaning and maintenance. Some supplemental tasks also involve determining format, content, and production approach within a budget, or discussing shot composition; the specific decision authority is checked against this position's division of labor, and it cannot be asserted that all technicians have no content or artistic involvement, nor can the organizer's final approval authority be obtained from the task list.

O*NET occupational identity and tasks: O*NET-SOC 27-4011.00 Audio and Video Technicians, page updated 2026, Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to below 7.0), and this occupation is not marked Bright Outlook. The official duties are to "set up, maintain, and strike audio and video equipment for live or recorded events, such as microphones, speakers, connecting cables, mixing and switching equipment, cameras, monitors, and servers and related electronic equipment, serving concerts, conferences, exhibitions, presentations, podcasts, press conferences, and sporting events"; there are 31 tasks in total, and the highly important tasks include notifying the supervisor when major repair is needed (77), diagnosing and handling media system faults (71), directing and coordinating assistant personnel during production (68), compressing and digitizing and storing audio and video data (68), and installing, adjusting, and operating recording, editing, and transmission equipment (67). The 31 tasks comprise 11 Core, 18 Supplemental, and 2 New; the supplemental tasks include determining the content approach 59 and script and graphics creativity 51, and the new tasks of drone photography and equipment procurement have no importance provided. There are also 41 general activities and 27 detailed activities; the new tasks do not represent drone operating authorization.

U.S. wage distribution: the 2025 BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) presented by O*NET, on the basis of Audio and Video Technicians (SOC 27-4011) — annual wage 10th percentile 37,990 USD, 25th percentile 46,390 USD, median 58,100 USD, 75th percentile 77,560 USD, and 90th percentile 100,650 USD; the corresponding median hourly wage is 27.93 USD.

Chinese wage reference: in 2025 the culture, sports, and entertainment industry urban non-private unit average was 129,447 yuan per year and the private unit average 64,015 yuan per year; leasing and business services were 110,162 and 68,919 yuan per year respectively. The former corresponds to performance and film and television activities and the latter to the equipment rental and exhibition employer background; both are national industry pre-tax averages, not the 27-4011 occupational median, starting pay, or take-home income.

BLS Table 1.2 lists this occupation's 2025 employment at 87600, the 2035 projection at 91100, a net increase of 3400, growth of 3.9%, and 6600 annual openings; each headcount column is rounded independently, and the openings include replacement demand from transfers and exits. paragraphs: This page compares audio and video technicians with five adjacent directions on the same set of dimensions: career direction, core work and output, key differences, and which direction suits each preference. The adjacent directions are described according to their own official occupational descriptions and do not mean the trade names are interchangeable.

Evidence note: the career directions and core outputs are based on the official descriptions of O*NET 27-4011.00 and adjacent entries and are on the U.S. basis; the qualification, authorization, and safety requirements of adjacent trades must be verified separately by their own jurisdiction, and this page does not present any direction as a shortcut to a career change.

The table below compares audio and video technicians with adjacent trades and the paths for moving in from adjacent positions; the basis for judgment is the main output, what the role is responsible for, and the training required, rather than how similar the trade names are.
Broadcast Technicians (27-4012.00)
Responsible for the transmission, transport, and broadcast links of broadcast signals, with stable broadcast signals as the main output.

Both master audio and video equipment and signal fundamentals; broadcast technicians face the broadcast link and transmission systems, while audio and video technicians face the setup, operation, and strike of live events.

If you would rather work on broadcast and transmission systems, look first at broadcast technicians; if you would rather do on-site system setup and watch duty, look first at audio and video technicians.
Sound Engineering Technicians (27-4014.00)

Sound engineering technicians may record, synchronize, mix, and reproduce sound for performances, film, television, podcasts, and events, with sound engineering and records as outputs; the work is not confined to the studio.

Sound engineering concentrates more on sound recording and mixing; audio and video technicians handle both video and on-site systems. Equipment and tasks may overlap, and the difference should be checked against the position's main output.

If you lean more toward sound recording and mixing, you can compare sound engineering; if you lean more toward audio and video system setup and watch duty, you can compare this occupation, checking the equipment and authorization separately.
Electrical and Electronic Engineering Technologists and Technicians (O*NET 17-3023.00)

Usually design, assemble, repair, and adjust electrical and electronic components, circuits, and control devices under the direction of engineers, providing drawings, prototypes, and test records for engineering evaluation.

These positions center on circuit and system-level design and testing and require corresponding professional training; audio and video technicians center on system integration of finished equipment and on-site troubleshooting.

If you would rather do circuit and system testing, look first at electronic and electrical engineering technicians; if you would rather do system integration and on-site watch duty, look first at audio and video technicians.
Computer Support Specialists
Provide software and hardware support for office and business systems, with usable office and network environments as the main output.

Computer support faces office and information systems and handles account, system, and network problems; audio and video technicians face on-site audio and video equipment and the signal chain and must handle power, interfaces, and site conditions.
If you would rather do office and system support, look first at computer support specialists; if you would rather do equipment and signal field work, look first at audio and video technicians.
Film and Video Editors (27-4032.00)
Edit and finish shot material, with finished films and project files as the main output.

Editors center on material organization, pacing, and post-production software and usually work in an editing room; audio and video technicians center on on-site equipment and signals and must face site and time pressure.
If you would rather do post-production editing and finishing, look first at film and video editors; if you would rather do on-site setup and operation, look first at audio and video technicians.
Moving in from an adjacent position or labor employment
You already have performance execution, equipment rental, camera assistant, or IT support experience and want to move to a complete audio and video technician position.

The gap is usually not equipment familiarity but the method for verifying the signal chain stage by stage, the fault location sequence, the safety procedures for electricity and rigging, the boundaries of materials and authorization, and the habit of recording handovers; having helped at a few events does not mean you can stand watch over a system independently.

If you are willing to start as an assistant and accept mentoring and review, you can consider moving in; if you only want to press buttons without learning the signal and safety procedures, the gap will be large.

Conclusion: the basis for choosing a direction is the main output, what the role is responsible for, and the training required, not how similar the names are; once the direction is set, check the target position's equipment system and training requirements, the actual working hours and project cycle, the authorization arrangements for electricity and rigging work, and the credit and use agreements for materials item by item, and keep written confirmation.

paragraphs: Students or career changers preparing to enter this occupation

Editorial study suggestion: first use paper materials to check the channel, test, and change records, then check the target position's equipment, training, and safety requirements; accept mentoring only after the on-site qualification and unit arrangements are in place, since study samples and certificates do not automatically prove work authority. Media, event, exhibition, and rental positions each require checking the contract and responsibilities.
Practicing audio and video technicians

Use digital tools in reviewable links such as equipment list and ledger management, channel and signal test records, material naming and archiving, and scheduling and work order flow; interface judgment, on-site troubleshooting, level and picture quality judgment, and electricity and rigging safety handling must still rest with people.
Event organizers and the technical team

Before introducing tools, clarify the links where they may be used, the knowledge scope for materials and site data, the authorization boundary for electricity and rigging work, and the responsible person for recording and review, so that any output returns to a traceable plan, test records, and the equipment ledger.
Education and development

Focus training on the signal chain and interfaces, stage-by-stage testing methods, the fault location sequence, on-site electricity and rigging safety, and material management and authorization boundaries, and also train the habit of checking tool output and the awareness to report abnormalities.

AI and automation may change records, material processing, and equipment operation. The BLS group page notes that technological advances may let broadcast, lighting, and sound systems operate with fewer technicians, while video conferencing and digital signage increase demand for audio and video technicians; these are different divisions of labor and cannot be summarized as the occupation never being replaced. The ILO2025 working paper builds a generative AI exposure index from occupational tasks and surveys and discusses the possibility of work transformation. The index measures task exposure, not this occupation's AI adoption rate, automation rate, unemployment probability, or job count projection.

Technical capability: equipment lists, transcoding, and material archiving can be trial targets for tools, and fault searches can assist with location; this is an editorial suggestion whose effectiveness must be tested in the field. Systems with sensors or networked inputs may receive on-site data, but data freshness, equipment status, and conditions must still be checked, and text output must not be treated as a safety conclusion.

Actual adoption: it requires unit permission, data and material authorization, stable inputs, and traceable manual work records. A software mention rate in job postings does not prove that AI is deployed, nor that watch personnel have been reduced; for critical operations the position lead must check authority and testing.

Employment outcome: BLS Table 1.2 lists SOC 27-4011: 87,600 employment in 2025 and a 2035 projection of 91,100, a ten-year net increase of 3,400 and growth of 3.9%, with 6,600 annual openings. Each headcount is rounded independently, and the net increase cannot be recalculated by subtracting the two displayed endpoints; the openings include replacement demand from transfers and exits, not net additions. This is an overall projection and not AI attribution. The AI discussion on the BLS group page concerns different trades, and an AI headcount reduction share for 27-4011 cannot be inferred from the exposure index or the overall growth.

Insufficient evidence: no occupation-level causal evidence that 27-4011 is wholly replaced by AI was obtained. Automation can change tasks and staffing; BLS discusses increased audio and video demand and reduced staffing needs for other technical systems separately, and cannot guarantee that this occupation will never be replaced.

paragraphs: Boundary: this section describes occupational risk and responsibility boundaries, not an evaluation of an individual or institution; the specific statutory obligations and handling procedures are determined by the applicable jurisdiction, the event plan, and the employment relationship.

Direct answer: the main risks include electric shock and tripping caused by temporary power and cable routing, falls and impacts from rigged and elevated equipment, interruption of the event caused by a signal chain fault, noise exposure and fatigue from long working hours, equipment damage and missing items at counting, and recording and use of materials beyond the authorized scope; control depends on the plan and checklist, stage-by-stage testing, qualified personnel carrying out electricity and rigging work, personal protection, and the abnormality reporting and escalation process.

Compiled from O*NET tasks and work context, the OSHA U.S. electrical safety overview, and the current Chinese Copyright Law; the risk judgments and control checklist are this page's editorial suggestions. Position exposure varies with the site, and the OSHA electrical overview does not prove Chinese rigging or hearing qualification requirements; specific tasks are checked separately by jurisdiction, equipment manual, and unit rules.
On-site technicians and site personnel
Improper temporary power, cable routing, and grounding may cause electric shock, equipment damage, or personal injury.

Editorial on-site checking: confirm the power conditions, capacity, grounding, and cable pathway protection according to the unit's plan, and refer the related professional judgments to the corresponding responsible personnel; special operations within the Chinese catalog are governed by Ministry of Emergency Management Order No. 19, effective 2026-06-01: Articles 3 and 4 require identification according to the catalog and training, assessment, and certification, and Article 36 requires the unit to verify that certificates are genuine and valid and to keep files. Whether a task falls under the catalog's electrician or work-at-height operations must be checked against the specific task; site approval and AV proficiency cannot replace statutory certificates, nor are ordinary signal cable connections all called special operations. U.S. 1910.333 requires de-energizing according to the hazard, verifying absence of voltage, and applicable lockout and tagout, and turning off with a button does not replace de-energizing, and this page does not teach unqualified readers to work on mains electricity.
Taking power at will to save time, running cables across pathways without protection, or unreliable grounding.

Improper rigging or elevated placement of speakers, lights, and stands may cause falls and impact injuries.

Test channel by channel, prepare a backup path, record the key parameters, and retest after a change.
Skipping testing and starting the show directly, or not re-verifying after a change.

Excessive noise may damage hearing, and continuous work requires a separate fatigue assessment; the O*NET noise question does not provide measured sound levels, and the industry name cannot be used to conclude that everyone exceeds limits or the degree of damage.

U.S. general industry 1910.95 requires employer monitoring and a hearing protection program according to exposure conditions, including applicable hearing tests; 85 dBA as an eight-hour TWA is an action level, not a measured value for this position or a Chinese threshold. Staying in a high sound pressure environment for a long time without wearing hearing protection.

Recording, copying, and distributing others' performances and works beyond the authorized scope may give rise to infringement liability.

Articles 38, 39, 42, and 43 of the Chinese Copyright Law distinguish the work, the performer's license, and remuneration and have corresponding statutory exceptions; the ownership of audiovisual and commissioned works is checked separately under Articles 17 and 19 and the contract. The editorial suggestion is to register the act, the material, the right, the term, and the public scope item by item, and a single permit from the organizer cannot cover all rights.

There is recording or distribution requiring a license without obtaining the corresponding license, or going beyond the contract scope, ignoring remuneration and the statutory exception conditions; it cannot be generalized that all use without an additional license is infringing.

Count from the checklist and register in and out of the warehouse, complete routine cleaning and maintenance, and report equipment that needs major repair.

subject.summary: This page covers audio and video technicians (O*NET-SOC 27-4011.00): setting up, maintaining, and striking audio and video equipment for on-site or recorded events, testing the signal chain, standing watch, handling faults, and recording the handover.
